title: Creating the Big Picture
subtitle: Turn shared direction into useful choices
summary: Four teams bring Pip incompatible APIs. A vision describes the useful future; strategy coordinates choices to reach it. Pip involves the affected teams and writes the reasoning so they can make compatible local decisions without queuing at one desk.

concepts.title: Vision
concepts.body: Four teams arrive with incompatible API plans. Pip asks what the workshop should make possible: teams safely evolving APIs without a central queue. That is a technical vision—a coherent future and why it matters to users and the organization. It connects the technical landscape to real needs. Colleagues can use it to decide what belongs in the future and what should gradually disappear.

steps.text: Pip asks what the future should enable.
Use the vision to decide what belongs and what can disappear.

concepts.title: Strategy
concepts.body: Pip’s vision earns nods, but the teams still need a route. Strategy chooses coordinated actions and priorities under present constraints, including what not to pursue. Compatibility first, migration next, deletion later: the sequence makes trade-offs visible. A shopping list of attractive technologies would not resolve competition for people, time, and attention. Pip starts from the workshop’s actual position rather than confusing the destination with the plan.

steps.text: Pip turns the destination into constrained choices.
Retire the old path when the transition is ready.

concepts.title: Alignment
concepts.body: Pip brings a polished proposal to the workshop; a team points out a constraint that breaks it. Next time, they work together earlier. Alignment means affected people share enough context to make compatible decisions without constant escalation. Participation can improve the plan and its ownership. Polite agreement with a document is weaker evidence than each team explaining how the shared API principle changes its next choice.

steps.text: Pip invites teams before finalizing the answer.
Their constraints can change the plan.

concepts.title: Writing
concepts.body: A colleague misses Pip’s meeting but still needs to decide. A written RFC carries the audience, purpose, proposed direction, requested response, and reasoning beyond that meeting. It preserves rejected alternatives and invites asynchronous challenge. Pip updates it when circumstances change. Writing creates institutional memory that can be reviewed and revisited; it does not require everyone to find Pip whenever a question appears.

steps.text: Pip writes for colleagues outside the original meeting.
Keep purpose, alternatives, and reasoning together.
Decisions do not depend on a permanent queue at Pip’s desk.

misconceptions.claim: a staff-plus role is mainly about applying a universal formula.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter treats judgment as contextual: identify forces, listen to evidence, and adapt the response to the actual system and people.

misconceptions.claim: A visible activity or artifact proves the work is complete.
misconceptions.correction: Completion requires a useful outcome, shared understanding, and a way to notice whether the decision worked over time.

scenario.title: Publish a direction
scenario.context: Four workshop teams bring Pip incompatible data APIs. One quarter remains to reduce duplication without centralizing every implementation choice.

options.label: Write vision and strategy
options.benefit: Teams share a direction while retaining local design decisions.
options.cost: Writing and discussion take time before implementation appears.
options.consequence: Pip works with owners on a short vision, principles, and staged strategy. Local designs can now converge without constant permission.

options.label: Issue a central design
options.benefit: A single design is quick to announce.
options.cost: Every exception needs another central ruling.
options.consequence: Edge cases accumulate at Pip’s desk. The announcement was fast; the workshop’s delivery is not.

scenario.debrief: Shared direction should help other people decide. Pip checks whether the artifact creates useful autonomy or a new approval queue.

quiz.question: Which statement is a vision rather than a task?
options: Teams can safely ship independent changes
quiz.explanation: A vision describes a coherent future state that can guide many decisions.

quiz.question: What turns a desired future into strategy?
options: Choosing actions and priorities under constraints
quiz.explanation: Strategy makes coordinated choices about reaching the destination.

quiz.question: Why involve affected teams before finalizing a technical direction?
options: Their constraints can improve the plan and its ownership
It removes the need to explain the decision
quiz.explanation: Early participation supplies context and builds shared understanding.

exercise.title: Make the next move legible
exercise.prompt: Describe a staff-level decision, the people and terrain involved, and the route by which you will learn whether it worked.
